Activity: Observe the picture about the development of atomic model and identify the model that: a. discovers electrons. b. proposes the orbits.

We have discussed the atom and Dalton’s atomic theory and its postulates in unit-2.1. In this unit we will discuss the structure of atoms in detail. Dalton postulated atom as a fundamental unit of matter which is indivisible. Later on, various experiments were conducted and concluded that the atom consists of a nucleus as a central core and negatively charged electron around the nucleus. In 1897 the British Physicist J.J Thomson discovered negatively charged electrons in the atom from his famous experiment using cathode ray tubes. Likewise, Rutherford discovered positively charged proton in 1911 from an alpha rays scattering experiment. In 1932 James Chadwick discovered a neutral particle in the atom called a neutron, the same mass as that of proton and much heavier than electron.

3.1 Rutherford’s atomic model and its limitations
Activity:
a. Create a circle with a center on the whiteboard. b. Soak 4-5 tennis balls in ink and throw each ball one by one

toward the center of the circle and aim to hit it. c. Observe and record the number of balls that successfully hit the center and those that do not. d. Examine the bouncing behavior of the balls and identify the causes of bouncing.

Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden conducted the experiment called Alpha particles scattering experiment in 1909 under the guidance of Ernest Rutherford. Based on these experiments Rutherford developed an atomic model called Ruther ford’s atomic model or nuclear model or planetary model.

Ernest Rutherford (18711937) was a New Zealand physicist has been known as ‘father of nuclear physics”. He made a significant contribution in the development of atomic model and proposing the concept of radioactivity and radioactive decay. He was awarded the Nobel prize in chemistry in 1908 for his investigation into disintegration of the elements.

Fig: Alpha particles scattering experiment These scientists observed the effect of bombarding thin gold foil with positively charged alpha particles (helium nuclei) on the zinc sulfide coated screen. They found that:
a. Most of the particles (99 %) passed through the foil without significant deflection as shown by green dots in the figure.
b. A small fraction of alpha particles experienced small angle deflections as in purple dots. c. Very few of them bounced back in the same direction of the source.
Figure: structure of gold atom according to rutherford Chemistry, Grade XI | 73
Conclusions of the Rutherford experiment:
a. Most of the alpha particles passes through the atom which indicates most of the space of the atom is empty.
b. Some of the particles deflected with some angle means there is a positively charged mass inside the atom.
c. Very few alpha particles bounced back or deflected with almost 180 0 angles meaning there is a dense mass concentrated in the small region inside an atom.
